```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Stomach contents are rarely identified to a single depth. A shrimp may be named
to species, a fish fragment only to "Teleostei", and a bolus of digested tissue
to nothing at all. DietView keeps every one of those records, attaches a
taxonomic lineage to it, and lets you look at the diet at all ranks at once,
with the material that could not be identified below a given rank kept in view.

This vignette runs one complete analysis on the example table that ships with
the package. The table is invented: 24 prey records from 11 stomachs of three
predators. That is enough to show every step and far too little to say anything
about what these fish eat, so read the numbers below as a demonstration of the
mechanics only. The vignette "A known diet" uses a larger simulated survey to
show what keeping unidentified records changes.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)
```

## 1. One row per prey record

```{r load}
dat <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
head(dat[, c("predator_species_common_name", "stomach_id", "verified_name",
             "prey_weight", "digestion_level_id")])
```

Each row is one prey taxon found in one stomach, with its wet weight in grams
and a digestion score from 1 (fresh) to 5 (unrecognizable). There are no
taxonomy columns. DietView adds them in step 3.

## 2. Say which column is which

```{r spec}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator   = "predator_species_common_name",
  stomach    = "stomach_id",
  prey_id    = "aphia_id",        # WoRMS AphiaID, used first when present
  prey_name  = "verified_name",   # scientific name, used when there is no ID
  weight     = "prey_weight",
  digestion  = "digestion_level_id",
  covariates = c("period", "region")
)
dv_validate(dat, spec)
```

The specification changes nothing in your table. It records which column plays
which role, so the original data never have to be renamed, and it can be saved
next to your results. `dv_validate()` stops if a declared column is missing or
a weight is negative, warns about records with no prey key, weights that are
not numbers and stomach IDs shared between predators, and ends with a one-line
description of the sample.

## 3. Attach the taxonomy

The example ships with a lineage table: one row per prey name, one column per
rank.

```{r lineage}
lin <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example_lineage.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
lin[lin$verified_name %in% c("Pandalus borealis", "Decapoda", "unidentified material"), ]
```

Look at how incomplete identifications are stored. `Decapoda` has an order but
no family, genus or species, and `unidentified material` has nothing. Those
empty cells are not errors. They record where identification stopped, and
DietView keeps them.

```{r prepare}
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lin, verbose = FALSE)
prep
```

With your own data you would normally query the World Register of Marine
Species once, read the matching report, and save the result as a lineage table
for every later run:

```{r worms, eval = FALSE}
prep_online <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")   # needs 'worrms' and an internet connection
dv_taxonomy_report(prep_online)                            # fuzzy and unresolved matches
```

Saving the lineage fixes the taxonomic snapshot your figures were made from.
Note the date and the `worrms` version alongside it, because WoRMS changes.

## 4. Count the diet at every rank

```{r tree}
tree <- dv_build_tree(prep$data, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
cls  <- dv_rank_table(tree, "Class")
cls
```

`value_occ` is the number of prey records assigned to each class, and `pct_occ`
its share of all records. `value_w` and `pct_w` do the same for weight. Every
record appears once in every ring of the tree: under the taxon it was
identified to at that rank or, if identification stopped earlier, in an `NA`
node below the last rank it reached. The denominator is therefore the same at
every rank, here all `r nrow(prep$data)` records or
`r round(sum(prep$data$prey_weight), 1)` g, and each ring adds up to 100%.

```{r fish, include = FALSE}
fish <- lin$class[lin$verified_name == "Ammodytes dubius"]   # the class holding the fish
stopifnot(length(fish) == 1, fish %in% cls$label)
```

The two currencies tell different stories. Malacostraca make up
`r round(cls$pct_occ[cls$label == "Malacostraca"], 1)`% of the records, and fish
(`r fish`) only `r round(cls$pct_occ[cls$label == fish], 1)`%, yet the
fish account for `r round(cls$pct_w[cls$label == fish], 1)`% of the
weight. Records tell you how often a kind of prey turns up; weight tells you how
much it contributes. Report both, or say which one you chose.

A note on names: `pct_occ` is a share of records. It is not the frequency of
occurrence (%FO) of the diet literature, which is the proportion of stomachs
containing a prey and does not add up across prey. `dv_fo_table()` gives %FO:

```{r fo}
fo <- dv_fo_table(prep, rank = "class")
fo[fo$taxon == "Malacostraca", ]
```

Malacostraca account for 11 of the 24 records but turn up in 7 of the 11
stomachs, because several stomachs hold more than one malacostracan.

## 5. How much was identified?

```{r na-share}
na_share <- sapply(prep$ranks, function(r) {
  tb <- dv_rank_table(tree, tools::toTitleCase(r))
  round(sum(tb$pct_occ[tb$label == "NA"]), 1)
})
na_share
```

In this table `r na_share[["order"]]`% of the records are unidentified at
order and `r na_share[["species"]]`% at species. A statement about species
would rest on fewer than half of the records, and digestion does not remove
prey at random, so that half is not a random sample. This is why DietView keeps
the unidentified nodes: they show how far a fine-rank statement can be trusted.

## 6. Draw it

```{r sunburst, eval = FALSE}
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", title = "All predators, share of prey records")
```

The figure is interactive, so it is drawn on the package website rather than in
this installed vignette. The center is the kingdom ring and each ring outward is
one rank finer. White wedges with gray edges are records not identified at that rank. Hovering shows the count and the share. When you compare panels, build
one palette from the pooled data and pass it to every panel (see the article on
covariates).

## 7. Digestion

```{r digestion}
dg <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep)
dg[, c("digestion", "finest_rank", "n_records", "p_records")]
```

For each digestion score, the table gives the share of records whose deepest
identified rank is species, genus, and so on, or none at all. With 24 records,
two of them at score 1 and two at score 5, it cannot show a trend; it only shows
the layout. The digestion vignette explains how to read it on real data.

## 8. Before you report

- State the currency of every percentage: records, numbers or weight.
- Report the unidentified share at the rank you discuss (step 5).
- Give the taxonomic source and its date, or archive the lineage table.
- If you aggregated rare prey (`dv_aggregate_threshold()`), give the threshold.
- Archive the specification and the code with the figures.
- Cite the package and the version you used. `citation("DietView")` gives the
  reference, "DietView: An R package for interactive, hierarchical
  visualization of predator stomach-content data".

## 9. Share it

```{r share, eval = FALSE}
dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "diet.html"),
              strata = c("period", "region"))
run_dietview(prep)   # interactive exploration, needs 'shiny'
```

The HTML file opens in any browser and needs neither R nor an internet
connection. It is a snapshot: it shows the data as they were when you built it.
